paper.title: The AES-CMAC Algorithm (RFC 4493; CMAC is the OMAC1 One-Key CBC-MAC of Iwata and Kurosawa, FSE 2003)

program.how: written for ounce-core from the algorithm in RFC 4493 section 2 and FIPS 197 AES (S-box computed by GF(2^8) inversion, AES-128/192/256 key schedules); no third-party code copied (the RFC's Appendix A test code was not used)
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: RFC 4493 Section 4: AES-128(K,0), subkeys K1 and K2, and the four tags (messages of 0, 16, 40 and 64 bytes) reproduce (7 of 7 values)

NIST's published CMAC examples for AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 (4 messages each: 0, 16, 20, 64 bytes): for each of the 12 examples the intermediate L = AES_K(0), the printed subkey (K1 or K2) and the tag match (36 of 36 values)

expected_values_source.what: RFC 4493 section 4 test vectors, and the NIST 'Block Cipher Modes of Operation: CMAC Mode for Authentication' example file (aes_cmac.pdf, parts CMAC-AES128/192/256), both parsed mechanically from the fetched texts
expected_values_source.note: the vectors are data, copied as numbers. The 128-bit RFC and NIST examples share keys and several messages; the 192/256-bit examples and the 20-byte message are only in the NIST file. The Iwata-Kurosawa paper itself was not fetched

negative_control: built with -DCMAC_RB=0x86 (field constant 0x86 instead of 0x87), 28 of 43 values match (the AES(K,0) values and tags of messages whose subkey path is unaffected) and the program exits 1; check.sh reports NOT REPRODUCED
not_checked: the security proofs of OMAC/CMAC, or any cryptanalysis
values printed in the Iwata-Kurosawa FSE 2003 paper (not fetched)
truncated tags, messages longer than 64 bytes or not of the listed lengths, and the TDEA CMAC examples in the NIST file
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about any hardware)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces exactly the values printed in RFC 4493 and in NIST's CMAC examples for the 16 listed message/key combinations. It does not show CMAC is secure.
